metaDescription: Six patio heaters compared on propane BTU, electric infrared wattage, safety shutoffs, base stability and wheels to help you stay warm on cool evenings outside.
introParagraphs: A patio heater is one of those purchases where the number on the box can mislead you. A big BTU rating sounds like more warmth, but real comfort depends on the reflector, the distance from the heater, the wind and your ceiling height. Electric infrared units behave very differently from propane towers, and the right choice depends far more on your space and your setup than on any single spec.

This lineup covers six heaters across both camps. The Sweetcrispy and Hykolity table models and the Amazon Basics burn propane at 46,000 to 50,000 BTU, the Hykolity Pyramid stands 90 inches tall with a glass flame tube, and one electric infrared option, the DR. INFRARED at up to 1500W, suits areas near an outlet. Propane heaters are for outdoors only, and only electric units rated for indoor use should ever be used inside.

We evaluated each one based on product specs and buyer feedback, concentrating on heat output, safety features, stability and how easy each is to move and light. Always follow the maker's clearance distances from flammables, awnings and low ceilings.

products.name: Sweetcrispy 48,000 BTU Propane Patio Heater
products.description:
The Sweetcrispy is a propane patio heater rated at 48,000 BTU, with a coverage claim of an 18 foot diameter for four to eight people. The burner uses a double-layer 304 stainless steel mesh that the listing says outperforms cheaper single-layer burners. Dual protection cuts gas if the flame blows out, and a tilt sensor shuts it off past 45 degrees.

A round built-in side table with a central cutout holds drinks and gives access to the valve. Wheels make it easy to roll to where guests are sitting, and ground anchors are included for uneven surfaces. The tradeoff is that rated coverage depends on wind, distance and ceiling height, so the 18 foot claim is best treated as a ceiling rather than a promise. It has no weighted base, and the listing names no certification.

For ownership, plan tank storage and check clearance distances in the manual, since a 20 pound tank is not included. The stainless mesh tends to hold up better through repeated heating cycles than single-layer grids. Compared with the Amazon Basics at 46,000 BTU and a 9 foot radius, it claims a larger footprint at slightly higher output. Compared with the Hykolity sand box model at 50,000 BTU, it is easier to roll but far less planted in wind.
products.bestFor: Open patios that want solid propane heat with flame-out protection.
pros: Flame-out cutoff plus 45 degree tilt sensor
Round side table with valve cutout
cons: No weighted base for breezy yards
Coverage is a ceiling and no certification is named

products.name: Hykolity 50,000 BTU Patio Heater With Sand Box Table
products.description:
The Hykolity sand box model delivers 50,000 BTU through a double-layer 304 stainless steel burner mesh and an umbrella-style top. Its conical base is described as more stable than a traditional round barrel, with a weight-adjustable fill the listing says was tested up to 26.45 pounds. The listing states coverage of up to 200 sq ft and a tilt system that extinguishes the flame past 45 degrees.

A table surface and wheels make it a practical hosting heater, and one-press ignition with a control valve keeps the controls simple. The ballast is the headline feature, because it prevents a fall rather than cutting gas after one starts. The tradeoff is that a filled base is heavy to reposition, and sand or water adds a setup step. Freezing weather can also be a problem for any liquid-filled base.

Assembly is described as under an hour, and the tank, which is not included, should stay upright and outdoors. Check the base fill before gusty evenings and drain it before a hard freeze. Compared with the Sweetcrispy at 48,000 BTU, it is the stronger choice in wind but harder to move. Compared with the Amazon Basics at 46,000 BTU, it adds about 4,000 BTU and a stated 200 sq ft figure.
products.bestFor: Breezier yards where a weighted base and tabletop help.
pros: 50,000 BTU with 200 sq ft stated coverage
cons: Filled base is heavy to move
Liquid ballast can freeze in winter

products.name: Amazon Basics 46,000 BTU Portable Propane Patio Heater
products.description:
The Amazon Basics heater is rated at 46,000 BTU and claims heat for up to a 9 foot radius. It has one-touch ignition, an adjustable temperature knob and a tilt safety valve that shuts the gas off automatically. A water box weighs down the base, and a chain is included to secure the tank.

The powder-coated slate gray finish is meant for lasting strength, and a wheel kit lets you roll it into place. It runs on a standard 20 pound propane tank that is not included. It is the simplest and most familiar tower in this group, with fewer extras than the Hykolity table models. That simplicity is also the tradeoff, since there is no table and no flame-out detail on the listing.

For ownership, fill the water box before use and drain it ahead of freezing weather so it cannot crack or freeze. Secure the tank with the chain and keep the whole unit clear of awnings and low ceilings. Compared with the Sweetcrispy at 48,000 BTU, it gives up a little output and the stainless burner. Compared with the Hykolity sand box model at 50,000 BTU, it uses a similar ballast idea with a clearer radius claim of 9 feet.
products.bestFor: Home patios that want a familiar, simple propane heater.
pros: Tilt shutoff valve and tank chain
cons: Water base can freeze in cold weather

products.name: Hykolity 48,000 BTU Pyramid Patio Heater With Cover
products.description:
The Hykolity Pyramid stands 90 inches tall and burns 48,000 BTU behind a clear glass tube with a visible flame. The listing says a 20 pound tank runs it for 8 to 10 hours, and a side door gives access to change the tank. It has variable heat settings, a built-in control valve and two detachable wheels.

An anti-tilt device shuts the heater off past 45 degrees, and a waterproof cover is included to protect it in bad weather. It is the decorative choice in the group, because the glass flame turns a heater into a centerpiece. The tradeoff is height, since 90 inches needs real clearance under a pergola, and the listing does not describe flame-out protection or a weighted base. A tall narrow tower also deserves level footing.

For ownership, the side door makes tank swaps easier than on towers where the tank is hidden behind a panel. Let it cool before covering it, and store it dry. Compared with the Sweetcrispy at 48,000 BTU, it matches the output but swaps the side table for a glass flame. Compared with the DR. INFRARED at 1500W, it covers an open patio while the electric unit warms only nearby seats.
products.bestFor: Open patios with high clearance where looks matter.
pros: Glass tube flame on a 90 inch pyramid
Side door for easy tank changes

products.name: DR. INFRARED Portable Infrared Patio Heater 1500W
products.description:
The DR. INFRARED is a flame-free heater with three power settings of 900W, 1200W and 1500W on a standard 120V plug. The listing gives it an IP55 rating for indoor and outdoor use and describes a mirror aluminum reflector with 90 percent reflectivity around a carbon lamp. Wall and ceiling mounting brackets are included.

Infrared heats people and objects directly rather than warming the air, so it handles a light breeze better than a flame. It avoids tanks, open fire and fuel storage altogether. The remote adjusts it from your seat, but it has no thermostat, so you set the level manually. The tradeoff is output, since 1500W warms a defined seating area and cannot match a 48,000 BTU tower across a wide patio.

For ownership, place it near your seats, route the cord safely and use a protected outlet. There is nothing to refill and almost nothing to clean. Compared with the Sweetcrispy at 48,000 BTU, it is cleaner and quieter but only effective at close range. Compared with the Hykolity electric at 1500W, it offers three settings and mounting brackets, while the Hykolity adds a timer and certification.
products.bestFor: Defined seating areas near an outlet where clean, flame-free heat matters.
pros: IP55 rating for indoor and outdoor use
cons: Limited to what a 120V outlet delivers
No thermostat or timer is listed

products.name: Hykolity 1500W Electric Infrared Patio Heater, 38.5 Inch
products.description:
The Hykolity electric heater is a 38.5 inch standing infrared unit with dual carbon heating tubes and two heat output levels, topping out at 1500W. A remote control and a 0 to 24 hour auto shut-off timer come with it, along with a one-touch button on the unit. The listing states an IP44 rating for indoor and outdoor use and ETL certified safety protection.

Tip-over auto shut-off and overheat protection are both described, and the heater restarts on its own when set upright again. That mix of a named certification and two cutoffs is rarer on listings than it should be. It is compact enough for a deck corner, a garage or a home office as well as a patio. The tradeoff is the same ceiling as every 120V unit: 1500W warms nearby seats, not a yard.

For ownership, the timer is the standout, since you can set it and leave without worrying about it running all night. Place it a safe distance from furniture and keep the cord out of walkways. Compared with the DR. INFRARED, it adds a timer and a certification, but it lacks the wall and ceiling brackets. Compared with the Hykolity Pyramid at 48,000 BTU, it is far weaker in open air but needs no tank.
products.bestFor: Small decks and garages that want a timer and a certified electric heater.
cons: IP44 is more splash-resistant than rainproof

buyingCriteria.explanation: Propane warms the air around a flame and suits open or lightly covered areas, while infrared heats people and objects directly and handles breeze better. Fuel-burning heaters are outdoor only because of carbon monoxide risk, and only electric units whose listings say indoor use should ever come inside. The Sweetcrispy at 48,000 BTU and the Hykolity Pyramid at 48,000 BTU cover open patios, while the DR. INFRARED at 1500W and the Hykolity electric at 1500W suit a single seating group. Choose by how big your space is and whether an outlet is nearby. Mixing the two in one yard is common.

BTU alone does not predict comfort, because reflector shape, distance, wind and ceiling height change what you feel. A rough rule of thumb is about 20 BTU per square foot with a buffer for breeze, but the maker's figure is the better guide. The Hykolity sand box lists 50,000 BTU and 200 sq ft, the Sweetcrispy lists 48,000 BTU and an 18 foot diameter, and the Amazon Basics lists 46,000 BTU and a 9 foot radius. Treat these as best-case numbers. Add a unit or move closer when it is cold and windy.

A gas heater should have tilt protection and ideally flame-out protection, and an electric unit should have tip-over and overheat cutoffs. The Sweetcrispy names both a flame-out cutoff and a 45 degree tilt sensor, the Amazon Basics lists a tilt valve and a tank chain, and the Hykolity Pyramid lists a 45 degree anti-tilt shutoff. The Hykolity electric adds ETL certification, tip-over and overheat shutoff. Confirm each feature on the product page before you buy. A shutoff reacts to a lean, so level footing still matters.

A tall narrow tower is the main tipping risk, and wind is the usual trigger. Ballast resists tipping directly, while anchors and shutoffs only help afterward or on soft ground. The Hykolity sand box has a weight-adjustable conical base, the Amazon Basics has a water box, and the 90 inch Hykolity Pyramid has neither. Fill liquid ballast before gusty evenings and drain it before freezing weather. On hard concrete, favor a weighted base over anchors.

Propane units need more clearance from awnings, railings, low ceilings and fabric than infrared units, so follow the manual's distances. Height matters here, since the Hykolity Pyramid stands 90 inches and the Hykolity electric only 38.5 inches. Keep a gas heater away from tents, fences and anything that can catch heat. Never run one in a garage, enclosed porch or under a low pergola. Place guests at the distance the maker recommends rather than leaning in.

Outdoor use means rain, so look for a rating rather than the word waterproof. A higher second digit in an IP rating means better water protection, so the DR. INFRARED at IP55 resists more than the Hykolity electric at IP44, and neither is submersion proof. Certification marks such as the ETL on the Hykolity electric matter, but only when the listing text actually states them. Cover or store any heater between uses. The Hykolity Pyramid includes a waterproof cover for this reason.

howWeEvaluated.title: Heat output
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated output and coverage. The Hykolity sand box leads at 50,000 BTU and 200 sq ft, the Sweetcrispy and Pyramid follow at 48,000, and the Amazon Basics lists 46,000 and a 9 foot radius. The two electric units are rated at up to 1500W and are not directly comparable to the towers.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety features
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at shutoffs, certifications and base weight. The Sweetcrispy lists flame-out and tilt protection, the Amazon Basics a tilt valve with a water base, and the Hykolity electric lists ETL certification with tip-over and overheat cutoffs. Missing detail counted against a pick.

howWeEvaluated.title: Stability and mobility
howWeEvaluated.description: Wheels and weighted bases were compared. The Sweetcrispy and Hykolity models have wheels, and the 90 inch Pyramid is the tallest. Taller units tip more easily.

howWeEvaluated.title: Setup and controls
howWeEvaluated.description: Ignition and controls were weighed. The Amazon Basics has one-touch ignition and an adjustable knob, the Hykolity electric adds a 0 to 24 hour timer, and the DR. INFRARED has a remote and three power levels. Lineup positioning is clear: the Hykolity electric leads on controls, and the Hykolity sand box leads on stability.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit and value
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched each heater to a type of space. Propane picks suit open patios, while the DR. INFRARED suits defined areas near an outlet. Listings with fewer details ranked lower.

faq.q: How many BTUs do I need for a patio heater?
faq.a: A common rule of thumb is about 20 BTU per square foot, plus extra for wind, but the maker's coverage figure is a better guide. The towers here run from 46,000 to 50,000 BTU. The Hykolity sand box lists 200 sq ft, while the Sweetcrispy claims an 18 foot diameter. Treat those as best-case numbers.

faq.q: Should I choose propane or electric infrared?
faq.a: Choose propane for an open patio without nearby outlets and electric infrared for a defined seating area close to power. Infrared heats people directly and handles breeze better, but 1500W cannot match a 48,000 BTU tower. The DR. INFRARED and the Hykolity electric both top out at 1500W. Many owners keep one of each.

faq.q: Can I use a patio heater indoors or in a garage?
faq.a: Never use a propane heater indoors, in a garage or in an enclosed porch, because of carbon monoxide risk. Only electric units whose listings state indoor use should come inside, such as the DR. INFRARED at IP55 or the Hykolity electric at IP44. Even then, follow the manual's clearance distances. Keep cords out of walkways.

faq.q: What safety features should a gas patio heater have?
faq.a: Look for tilt shutoff and flame-out protection, and confirm both on the listing. The Sweetcrispy names both, while the Amazon Basics lists a tilt valve and the Hykolity Pyramid an anti-tilt shutoff. A shutoff only reacts once the heater is leaning, so a stable base and level footing matter just as much. Keep the tank upright and outdoors.

faq.q: How do I stop a tall heater tipping in wind?
faq.a: Use ballast, anchors and shelter together. The Hykolity sand box and Amazon Basics both fill their bases with weight, and the Sweetcrispy includes ground anchors. Anchors do not work on hard concrete, so a weighted base is the better choice on pavers. Drain liquid ballast before freezing weather.

faq.q: How long does a propane tank last in a patio heater?
faq.a: The Hykolity Pyramid listing says a 20 pound tank runs for 8 to 10 hours at its 48,000 BTU rating. Turning the control valve down stretches that, and a lower setting suits mild evenings. Keep a spare tank on hand for long gatherings. Store tanks upright and outdoors, never in a cover or enclosure.

faq.q: Do patio heaters need a cover?
faq.a: A cover protects the burner, finish and glass from rain and sun. The Hykolity Pyramid includes a waterproof cover, and other towers can use a separate one. Always let the heater cool fully before covering it. IP ratings such as IP44 or IP55 describe splash resistance, not permission to leave a heater in a storm.
